summary: Rocky Mountain National Park's only surviving fire lookout: a 1932 NPS rustic stone-and-frame tower on Shadow Mountain, closed to the public since 2015.

facts.design: NPS rustic L-4 cab with catwalk on a three-story stone and frame tower, San Francisco Landscape Architecture Division design

staffing.status: paid staff and volunteers, only during high fire severity (per NHLR)

access.note: Public access closed since 2015 due to deterioration (Rocky Mountain Conservancy)

visit.trail_note: Reached by a five-mile rugged hike; the tower is closed to the public, so it should not be climbed.

events.note: Phone line run to the summit from Grand Lake Ranger Station so the site could be used for fire detection

Built to NPS San Francisco Landscape Architecture Division design; construction first planned for 1931, bids too high; NHLR summary says completed 1934, its history says completed 1933; builder disputed (CCC labor per Wikipedia, local contractor per Conservancy)
NHLR: in service until 1969; Conservancy: in use until the late 1960s. Wikipedia gives 1978 as the last summer season of use
Added to National Register August 2, 1978 per Wikipedia and NPS record; NHLR says 1987
Conservancy-funded repairs to stairway and balcony
Registered with the National Historic Lookout Register August 13, 2003
Public access closed due to deterioration
NHLR: cab exterior in poor condition; stone tower in poor condition; decking and support beams rotted
Historical structure report (2020/2021) funded by Conservancy
Construction design plan for rehabilitation options (2022/2023)

evidence.supports: 1930 phone line to summit for fire detection
evidence.quote: The site was first used for fire detection in 1930 when a phone line was run to the summit from Grand Lake Ranger Station.

evidence.supports: built 1932 to NPS San Francisco design; regarded as among best NPS rustic buildings
evidence.quote: built in Rocky Mountain National Park in 1932, to the design of the National Park Service San Francisco Landscape Architecture Division.

evidence.supports: one of the best NPS rustic buildings
evidence.quote: It was regarded as one of the best National Park Service Rustic buildings in the national park system.

evidence.supports: construction planned for 1931, bids too high
evidence.quote: Construction of the rustic L-4 cab (NPS design) with catwalk was to begin in1931, but the bids were too high.

evidence.supports: work began 1932, stone tower finished the following year
evidence.quote: Work got under way in 1932 on the two story natural stone tower and was completed the following year.

evidence.supports: Wikipedia says CCC labor built it
evidence.quote: The lookout was built by Civilian Conservation Corps labor.

evidence.supports: Conservancy says a local contractor built it in 1932
evidence.quote: The Shadow Mountain Fire Lookout, built by a local contractor in 1932, emerged from this fire management philosophy.

evidence.supports: early rangers staffed the tower several days at a time
evidence.quote: During the Shadow Mountain Fire Lookout’s early years, male rangers staffed the tower for several days at a time.

evidence.supports: rangers watched for smoke, daily reports, maintenance
evidence.quote: They looked for signs of fire, sent daily reports, and handled maintenance tasks.

evidence.supports: married couples served as seasonal residents after WWII
evidence.quote: After WWII, married couples began serving as seasonal residents.

evidence.supports: first floor visitor contact, second floor staff quarters, usually a married couple
evidence.quote: The first floor has been used for visitor contact, while the second floor has been used as employee accommodation, usually for a married couple who would keep watch and deal with the public.

evidence.supports: in service until 1969 (NHLR)
evidence.quote: The lookout was in service until 1969 and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1987.

evidence.supports: use until late 1960s, shift from fire suppression to prescribed burns
evidence.quote: The tower remained in use until the late 1960s, when the NPS moved away from strict fire suppression and towards the introduction of prescribed burns.

evidence.supports: last summer season of use 1978 (Wikipedia)
evidence.quote: The last summer season for use was 1978.

evidence.supports: NRHP listing August 2, 1978
evidence.quote: Added to NRHP August 2, 1978

evidence.quote: In the past, the Conservancy has funded repairs to the tower’s stairway and balcony (1996), followed by a historical structure report (2020/2021), and a construction design plan for rehabilitation options (2022/2023).

evidence.supports: around $300,000 committed by Conservancy and donors
evidence.quote: To date, the Conservancy and its donors have committed around $300,000 to preserve this iconic structure.

evidence.supports: planned work to stabilize foundation and remove rotting stairway and railings
evidence.quote: The Conservancy’s Conservation Corps will work alongside the park’s historic preservation crew to stabilize the masonry stone foundation and remove the rotting stairway and railings leading to the upper floors.

evidence.supports: nearly two thousand hikers a year on five-mile hike
evidence.quote: Each year, nearly two thousand hikers make the five-mile rugged hike up the mountain to visit the tower.

corrections.proposed: closed (public access closed since 2015 due to deterioration)
corrections.why: Rocky Mountain Conservancy states the tower has been closed to public access since 2015.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikipedia, NPS record and the Conservancy give 1932 as the build year. The NHLR history gives 1932 to 1933 for construction, but its summary says 1934; the story uses 1932 and reports the rest.
Wikipedia and the NPS record give August 2, 1978; the NHLR gives 1987. The story uses 1978, the date the two non-register sources agree on.
